title: Copperlane Security review: SSO, KMS, Audit & Deployment options
topics: SSO / SAML integration and IdP choices
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs
summary: Intro discovery focused on security posture requirements for an inference deployment. Copperlane's main concerns: corporate SOC2 scope, SSO integration with Okta, customer-managed KMS for key separation, detailed audit logs for model requests, and clarity on data retention policies. Redwood AE + SE covered Hosted/Dedicated/Private options and proposed POC benchmarks. Action items: send SOC2/ISO docs, KMS integration doc, sample audit log format; schedule technical POC with Copperlane infra team next week.
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-12-05 16:30 UTC; Duration: ~52 minutes; Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (CISO, Copperlane), Liam O'Connor (Cloud Architect), Priya Kapoor (DevOps).

[00:00] Avery: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, um this is Avery from Redwood, joining with Diego on the technical side. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya: good thanks, uh tight day but ready to dig in.
[00:18] Liam: same here, thanks for fitting us in.
[00:22] Diego: great. quick agenda, we wanted to run through security posture — SOC2/ISO status, SSO and saml specifics, kms and encryption, audit logs, and then deployment choices (hosted, dedicated, private). we'll surface any gaps early.
[00:36] Priya: sounds good. For context, Copperlane is evaluating inference for PII-sensitive workflows across their claims processing pipeline. compliance is, like, a hard stop for us.
[00:48] Avery: thanks, that's useful. could you share your timeline and success criteria?
[00:52] Maya: timeline is Q1 pilot, scale in Q2 if pilot passes. success is: 1) pass SOC2 vendor review, 2) SSO integration with Okta + SAML, 3) customer-managed KMS, and 4) detailed per-request audit logs retained for 12 months.
[01:10] Diego: okay good, that's pretty clear. a quick note, our hosted API is SOC2 compliant and we have ISO 27001 scope for our control plane — we can send certs. for KMS we support both Redwood-managed keys and customer-managed keys via cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK).
[01:34] Maya: two quick questions: (1) can we bring our own HSM or do you only integrate with cloud KMS? (2) how granular is RBAC, we need least-privilege for teams and auditors
[01:45] Diego: for (1) we primarily integrate with cloud KMS via CMEK; for HSM on-prem it's possible with our Private deployment but that would be a separate eng engagement — Diego: basically you get a customer-managed key in your KMS and we never persist plaintext. for (2) RBAC is per-organization, per-project and per-route level; we expose roles via our console and API and you can tie it to SSO groups.
[02:12] Liam: do you support SCIM for group sync? our Okta set-up expects SCIM to map groups to roles automatically.
[02:18] Avery: yes, SCIM is supported for group sync; SAML for SSO and SCIM for provisioning. in some older notes it shows as 'SAML + SCIM', sorry sometimes the transcript auto-mangles that to 'sam-el' in our notes.
[02:30] Maya: (laughs) yep I've seen that. ok audit logs — we need per-request metadata including request_id, user_id, model_version, prompt_hash, and response_status. is that available?
[02:42] Diego: we can emit structured audit events with those fields; our default retention is 90 days in hosted but for enterprise customers we have extended retention add-ons and can ship logs to customer S3 buckets or to your SIEM via secure transfer.
[02:58] Priya: shipping logs off is important — we need logs in our own S3 account. also encryption — are logs encrypted server-side with our key?
[03:08] Diego: yes, when logs are exported to your S3 we can encrypt with your CMEK. in-hosted storage logs are encrypted at rest with provider keys; for full separation we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[03:22] Maya: what's the typical difference in SLA/latency/cost between hosted and dedicated? we worry about latency in peak loads.
[03:30] Avery: hosted is the fastest time-to-value and lower operational overhead; dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity and better latency predictability — cost is higher because you reserve capacity. Private gives you full network isolation and control (VPC or on-prem) and is the most work to set up.
[03:48] Liam: if we go Hosted but require CMEK and export logs to our S3, does that satisfy our audit team?
[03:55] Diego: usually yes, but audit teams sometimes insist on physical control or dedicated tenancy — that's a case-by-case. we can provide logs, attestations, and run through the SOC2 report.
[04:06] Maya: speaking of SOC2, we need the full vendor SOC2 report and an ISO scope statement. can you provide the latest reports?
[04:14] Avery: absolutely, we'll send the SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 evidence, redacted as needed.
[04:19] Priya: about RBAC: do you support role separation for operators vs model owners vs billing? we need separate access for billing so auditors can't see prompts.
[04:27] Diego: yes, roles are configurable; we also support token-level scoping so you can issue keys that only allow embeddings vs generation or limit by model. that helps with least privilege.
[04:40] Liam: how do you handle KV cache / prefix cache with privacy? our model uses sensitive prefixes, does Redwood persist KV cache?
[04:49] Diego: KV cache is ephemeral in the runtime; we don't persist long-term by default. for Dedicated/Private, you control caching policies and can ensure no persistent storage of caching layers.
[05:02] Maya: ok good. next, legal wants clarity on data retention: we need to confirm that prompts will not be used to train models and what your data deletion SLA is.
[05:12] Avery: our standard policy for enterprise customers is that we do not use customer data to train models; we can contractually forbid training usage. deletion SLA depends on deployment: hosted with standard retention — we can set deletion windows; Dedicated/Private gives you more immediate control since data can be routed to your account. we'll share the exact deletion SLA matrix.
[05:31] Priya: any E2E encryption for in-transit? we run strict mam — TLS is standard but do you support mutual TLS for API calls?
[05:38] Diego: mutual TLS is supported for Dedicated/private endpoints; hosted supports TLS 1.2+ with strong ciphers and client certs for admin APIs. we'll include the network diagram.
[05:50] Maya: if we consider a Private on-prem install, what's the rough timeline and scope?
[05:56] Avery: Private is an eng-heavy engagement — usually 6-10 weeks for initial deployment depending on environment. Dedicated (VPC) is 2-4 weeks. Hosted is immediate.
[06:06] Liam: ok let's talk about the POC — we want to run performance benchmarks and audit log verification. can Redwood generate a sample audit log stream for our team to ingest?
[06:16] Diego: yes we can generate synthetic traffic and deliver log streams in your S3 or SIEM for ingestion testing.
[06:23] Priya: we need request tracing to tie logs back to user sessions — header propagation?
[06:29] Diego: we include request_id and trace_id headers; you can correlate with your app logs.
[06:34] Maya: any external pen-test or vulnerability reports? our risk team will ask.
[06:38] Avery: we conduct third-party pen tests annually and can provide summaries and remediation history. full findings are shared under NDA.
[06:47] Liam: a small nit — for SAML assertions, do you require specific NameID formats? we use email as NameID.
[06:54] Diego: email NameID is supported, and we can map attributes via SCIM/claims mapping.
[06:59] Maya: what about long-term retention of embeddings or derivatives? does Redwood ever store embeddings by default?
[07:06] Diego: we store embeddings only if you enable embedding persistence. for hosted, default is transient; we can enable long-term storage in your S3 or in dedicated project buckets if required.
[07:19] Priya: cost question — how does CMEK impact cost? is there per-request KMS usage costing?
[07:25] Avery: yes CMEK means KMS API calls for envelope encryption; those have per-call costs from your cloud provider — usually negligible relative to GPU costs, but we'll provide an estimate.
[07:36] Maya: ok can you walk through an example audit log line?
[07:40] Diego: sure — sample: {timestamp, request_id, user_group, model, model_version, prompt_hash, token_count_in, token_count_out, response_status, route}. we'll send a CSV/json example.
[07:55] Liam: for our compliance we need immutable logs for at least 12 months and tamper evidence. can you sign logs or provide write-once storage guidance?
[08:03] Diego: we can export logs to a write-once S3 bucket with object lock and provide signatures via our log pipeline.
[08:12] Maya: what's your incident notification SLA? if there's a breach or misconfiguration, how quickly do we find out?
[08:19] Avery: incident triage notified within 2 hours; detailed report and remediation plan in 72 hours for high-severity incidents under our enterprise SLA.
[08:30] Priya: ok one more — audit access for external auditors, can they be granted read-only console access or do you provide a co-packaged bundle of artifacts?
[08:39] Diego: we support both: time-limited read-only access and curated evidence packs (logs, configs, certs) for auditors.
[08:46] Maya: cool. anything else re: encryption lifecycle?
[08:49] Diego: keys are rotated per your policy, and we support automatic or manual rotation. ephemeral session keys are used in the runtime.
[08:58] Avery: just to summarize at high level: Hosted — fastest but shared tenancy; Dedicated — reserved capacity, better isolation; Private — full isolation and customer-managed infra including on-prem HSMs.
[09:12] Maya: good. can you confirm whether the hosted environment is in multi-tenant compute but with logical separation?
[09:19] Diego: yes multi-tenant compute but logical separation, per-tenant encryption and process isolation. for strict tenant isolation you'd want Dedicated or Private.
[09:29] Liam: what's the billing model for Dedicated? is it committed monthly for units?
[09:33] Avery: yes monthly reserved capacity with burst options, we'll include the SKU/pricing in the follow-up.
[09:40] Maya: legal will also ask about sub-processors and their SOC2 coverage.
[09:45] Avery: we'll provide a sub-processor list and their attestation statuses.
[09:49] Priya: ok great.
[09:52] (brief pause)
[10:00] Diego: i'll note technical POC steps: 1) Redwood provisions a test project, 2) generate synthetic load and audit logs, 3) test KMS/CMEK key usage and log export, 4) run latency benchmarks against your sample workloads.
[10:16] Liam: that matches our asks. do you need a network diagram from us?
[10:19] Diego: yes a network diagram and the Okta tenant details (SCIM and SAML metadata) will help.
[10:24] Maya: I'll get legal to share a redacted network diagram and the compliance checklist we'll use.
[10:30] Avery: perfect — next steps we'll capture and share. any final questions?
[10:36] Priya: just one: for PII masking / redaction, do you have built-in tools or recommended patterns?
[10:43] Diego: we have pre-processing helpers for redaction and we recommend client-side masking before sending highly sensitive PII. we can advise on strategies during the POC.
[10:52] Maya: thanks, this was helpful.
[10:55] Avery: thank you all. we'll send the SOC2 and ISO docs, the KMS integration guide, sample audit logs, and a proposed POC plan by end of day Tuesday.
[11:06] (end of call)

Notes about transcription: occasional mishears ("sam-el" for SAML), speaker labels approximate, some filler removed for brevity.

Recap from Redwood: we will provide SOC2 Type II and ISO artifacts, sub-processor list, KMS/CMEK integration docs, sample structured audit log schema, SIEM/S3 export examples, SCIM/SAML configuration steps, and a POC plan that includes synthetic traffic and log export verification.
